theory.intro: A logarithm is an index, so the **log laws** come from the index laws: adding logs matches multiplying, subtracting matches dividing, and a coefficient matches a power. Every answer here stays written as a logarithm, not evaluated.
facts: **Product law:** $\log_{a}(mn)=\log_{a}m+\log_{a}n$ — a sum of logs becomes the log of a product.
**Quotient law:** $\log_{a}\!\left(\frac{m}{n}\right)=\log_{a}m-\log_{a}n$ — a difference of logs becomes the log of a quotient.
**Power law:** $\log_{a}(m^{n})=n\log_{a}m$ — a coefficient in front of a log is an index on its argument.
The product and quotient laws only apply when every logarithm has the **same base**.
The laws work both ways: left to right **expands** one log into several, right to left **combines** several into one.
A coefficient and an index are interchangeable, so $3\log_{a}2=\log_{a}2^{3}=\log_{a}8$.

For real logarithms, every argument must be positive and the base must satisfy $a>0$ and $a\ne1$. In these laws, $m>0$ and $n>0$ for products and quotients; in the power law, the underlying argument $m>0$ and the index $n$ can be any real number. These conditions apply to all questions here.
steps: Check that every logarithm being combined has the same base.

When combining, turn any coefficient into an index, multiply arguments for a sum of logs, and divide arguments for a difference of logs. When expanding, write the log of a product as a sum of logs, the log of a quotient as a difference of logs, and bring an index down as a coefficient.
Write the result as a single logarithm when combining, or as separate log terms when expanding.

workedExamples.solution_text:
Use the product law; keep the base unchanged.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\log_{7}4+\log_{7}5\\&=\log_{7}(4\times5)\\&=\log_{7}20\end{aligned}$

Use the quotient law, dividing the first argument by the second.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\log_{9}28-\log_{9}4\\&=\log_{9}\left(\frac{28}{4}\right)\\&=\log_{9}7\end{aligned}$

Use the power law to turn the coefficient into an index.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}3\log_{a}5\\&=\log_{a}(5^{3})\\&=\log_{a}125\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: Expand $\log_{a}(4z)$ as a sum of logarithms.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Use the product law in the opposite direction.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\log_{a}(4z)\\&=\log_{a}4+\log_{a}z\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: Expand $\log_{a}\left(\frac{r}{s}\right)$ as a difference of logarithms.
Expand $\log_{a}(z^{6})$ as a multiple of a logarithm.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Bring the index down as a coefficient.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\log_{a}(z^{6})\\&=6\log_{a}z\end{aligned}$

Write the argument as a power of $2$, then use the power law.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\log_{a}32\\&=\log_{a}(2^{5})\\&=5\log_{a}2\end{aligned}$

Combine the sum using the product law, then the difference using the quotient law.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\log_{7}6+\log_{7}5-\log_{7}3\\&=\log_{7}(6\times5)-\log_{7}3\\&=\log_{7}30-\log_{7}3\\&=\log_{7}\left(\frac{30}{3}\right)\\&=\log_{7}10\end{aligned}$

Turn both coefficients into indices before combining the logarithms.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{1}{2}\log_{a}16+2\log_{a}5\\&=\log_{a}(16^{\frac{1}{2}})+\log_{a}(5^{2})\\&=\log_{a}4+\log_{a}25\\&=\log_{a}(4\times25)\\&=\log_{a}100\end{aligned}$

The index $\frac{1}{3}$ gives a cube root.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{1}{3}\log_{a}64+\log_{a}5\\&=\log_{a}(64^{\frac{1}{3}})+\log_{a}5\\&=\log_{a}4+\log_{a}5\\&=\log_{a}(4\times5)\\&=\log_{a}20\end{aligned}$

Use the power law first, then the quotient law.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}3\log_{a}3-\log_{a}9\\&=\log_{a}(3^{3})-\log_{a}9\\&=\log_{a}27-\log_{a}9\\&=\log_{a}\left(\frac{27}{9}\right)\\&=\log_{a}3\end{aligned}$

Apply the power law, then combine the product and quotient.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}2\log_{7}4+\log_{7}3-\log_{7}8\\&=\log_{7}(4^{2})+\log_{7}3-\log_{7}8\\&=\log_{7}16+\log_{7}3-\log_{7}8\\&=\log_{7}(16\times3)-\log_{7}8\\&=\log_{7}48-\log_{7}8\\&=\log_{7}\left(\frac{48}{8}\right)\\&=\log_{7}6\end{aligned}$
